units.text: INT. EARNEST - CONTINUOUS
Do you suggest, Miss Fairfax, that I entrapped Ernest into an engagement? How dare you? This is no time for wearing the shallow mask of manners. When I see a spade I call it a spade.
units.name: CECILY

units.text: Satirically.
I am glad to say that I have never seen a spade. It is obvious that our social spheres have been widely different.
units.name: GWENDOLEN

units.text: Enter Merriman, followed by the footman.
He carries a salver, table cloth, and plate stand.
Cecily is about to retort.
The presence of the servants exercises a restraining influence, under which both girls chafe.
Shall I lay tea here as usual, Miss?
units.name: MERRIMAN

units.text: Sternly, in a calm voice.
Yes, as usual.
units.name: CECILY

units.text: Merriman begins to clear table and lay cloth.
A long pause.
Cecily and Gwendolen glare at each other.
Are there many interesting walks in the vicinity, Miss Cardew?
units.name: GWENDOLEN

units.text: Oh! yes! a great many. From the top of one of the hills quite close one can see five counties.
units.name: CECILY

units.text: Five counties! I don’t think I should like that; I hate crowds.
units.name: GWENDOLEN

units.text: Sweetly.
I suppose that is why you live in town?
units.name: CECILY

units.text: Gwendolen bites her lip, and beats her foot nervously with her parasol.
Looking round.
Quite a well-kept garden this is, Miss Cardew.
units.name: GWENDOLEN

units.text: So glad you like it, Miss Fairfax.
units.name: CECILY

units.text: I had no idea there were any flowers in the country.
units.name: GWENDOLEN

units.text: Oh, flowers are as common here, Miss Fairfax, as people are in London.
units.name: CECILY

units.text: Personally I cannot understand how anybody manages to exist in the country, if anybody who is anybody does. The country always bores me to death.
units.name: GWENDOLEN

units.text: Ah! This is what the newspapers call agricultural depression, is it not? I believe the aristocracy are suffering very much from it just at present. It is almost an epidemic amongst them, I have been told. May I offer you some tea, Miss Fairfax?
units.name: CECILY

units.text: With elaborate politeness.
Thank you.
units.name: GWENDOLEN

units.text: Aside.
Detestable girl! But I require tea!
units.name: GWENDOLEN

units.text: Sweetly.
Sugar?
units.name: CECILY

units.text: Superciliously.
No, thank you. Sugar is not fashionable any more.
units.name: GWENDOLEN

units.text: Cecily looks angrily at her, takes up the tongs and puts four lumps of sugar into the cup.
Severely.
Cake or bread and butter?
units.name: CECILY

units.text: In a bored manner.
Bread and butter, please. Cake is rarely seen at the best houses nowadays.
units.name: GWENDOLEN

units.text: Cuts a very large slice of cake, and puts it on the tray.
Hand that to Miss Fairfax.
units.name: CECILY

units.text: Merriman does so, and goes out with footman.
Gwendolen drinks the tea and makes a grimace.
Puts down cup at once, reaches out her hand to the bread and butter, looks at it, and finds it is cake.
Rises in indignation.

You have filled my tea with lumps of sugar, and though I asked most distinctly for bread and butter, you have given me cake. I am known for the gentleness of my disposition, and the extraordinary sweetness of my nature, but I warn you, Miss Cardew, you may go too far.
units.name: GWENDOLEN

units.text: Rising.
To save my poor, innocent, trusting boy from the machinations of any other girl there are no lengths to which I would not go.
units.name: CECILY

units.text: From the moment I saw you I distrusted you. I felt that you were false and deceitful. I am never deceived in such matters. My first impressions of people are invariably right.
units.name: GWENDOLEN

units.text: It seems to me, Miss Fairfax, that I am trespassing on your valuable time. No doubt you have many other calls of a similar character to make in the neighbourhood.
units.name: CECILY

units.text: Enter Jack.
Catching sight of him.
Ernest! My own Ernest!
units.name: GWENDOLEN
